lines.text: In 1925, a con man sold the Eiffel Tower, all seven thousand tons of it, to a scrap dealer.
You see, the tower was rusting, and lots of Parisians wanted it gone.
So Victor Lustig faked government letterhead and invited Paris's top scrap dealers to a fancy hotel.
He posed as an official from the Ministry of Posts and Telegraphs.
The tower was being sold for scrap, he said. Top secret.
Then he gave them a limousine tour, hunting for the hungriest buyer.
He picked André Poisson, new in town and desperate to be a big shot.
Even Poisson's wife thought it smelled fishy.
Yet Poisson paid, and Lustig fled to Austria with seventy thousand francs.
And Poisson was too embarrassed to call the police.
So Lustig came back to sell the tower again.
This time, a dealer called the police, and Lustig fled to America.
So why did Poisson ignore his own wife?
You see, Lustig asked him for a bribe.
He sighed that officials earn next to nothing, so Poisson slipped him cash.
A fake would never dare. So Poisson knew he was real.
It's like a bouncer asking twenty bucks to skip the line. You never doubt he works there.
Eleven years later, he was on Alcatraz. He died a prisoner in 1947.
The man who sold the Eiffel Tower? His death certificate lists his job as "apprentice salesman and counterfeiter."
